FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative timing. This simple rule creates a predictable and stable system where the earliest entry is always served first.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the most recent job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any process from waiting indefinitely for a slot that is already occupied by a newer job.

A practical example involves a server managing a batch of incoming web requests. If a new client connects at 10:00 AM, the system immediately serves that request before processing requests from 10:01 AM. This ensures that the most active user gets attention first, even if their request arrives later in the day.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. It treats all processes equally by prioritizing those who arrived earliest, preventing any single process from dominating the system. This makes it ideal for real-time applications where consistent response times are critical.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process waiting in the queue is blocked by a newer job that has already been served. This can cause delays for the waiting process, especially if the queue is long or the system is under load. However, this limitation is often acceptable in many real-world scenarios where responsiveness is more important than strict fairness.

Compared to other policies like Round Robin, FIFO provides better performance for time-sensitive tasks. Round Robin processes jobs sequentially but may not handle long queues efficiently. FIFO eliminates the overhead of maintaining a rotating list, making it faster for large batches of requests.

In summary, FIFO scheduling offers a robust foundation for scheduling systems by ensuring fair treatment and predictable execution. While it has limitations regarding blocking, its simplicity and efficiency make it a widely used choice in computer science and operating systems.
